title: Mechanics

sources.title: Faculty of Mathematics, University of Cambridge: Schedules of Lecture Courses and Form of Examinations, Mathematical Tripos 2026-27
sources.used_for: non-examinable status, intended audience, Michaelmas timing, the ten lecture titles (lectures 5 and 6 on dynamics of particles are merged into one topic here) and its role as background for Dynamics and Relativity

about: Mechanics is a short non-examinable course of ten Michaelmas Term lectures in Part IA of the Cambridge Mathematical Tripos, intended for students who have done only a limited amount of mechanics at A-level or equivalent. Following the official schedule it runs from kinematics and the equilibrium of particles and rigid bodies through the dynamics of particles (including projectiles with air resistance), energy, momentum, springs and simple harmonic motion, to motion in a circle. It is not examined itself, but the examinable Lent course Dynamics and Relativity assumes familiarity with it, so the questions here are practice for that course rather than for a Mechanics paper.
topics: Dynamics of particles, including projectiles with air resistance
Springs, strings and simple harmonic motion

notes.body:
The Part IA Mechanics course is a short, non-examinable bridging course of ten Michaelmas lectures. It is aimed at students who took little mechanics at A-level (or equivalent), and it covers the material that the examinable Lent course, Dynamics and Relativity, assumes you already know. If you did plenty of mechanics at school, treat this pack as a quick check of the basics. The schedule simply calls the first lecture a brief introduction; the modelling vocabulary and units below are standard background rather than listed schedule items.

Modelling vocabulary
Mechanics problems are idealised models of the real world. The standard words have precise meanings:
- Particle: a body whose size can be ignored, so all its mass acts at one point and it cannot rotate.
- Rigid body: a body of finite size whose shape does not change; it can rotate, so moments matter.
- Light: of negligible mass (a light string has the same tension throughout if nothing acts along it).
- Inextensible: a string that does not stretch, so connected particles share the same speed and acceleration.
- Smooth: frictionless. A smooth pulley does not change the tension in a string passing over it.
- Uniform: mass evenly distributed, so a uniform rod's centre of mass is at its midpoint.
- Rough: friction may act.

Units and dimensions
- SI base units for mechanics: kilogram (kg), metre (m), second (s). Derived units: newton N = kg m s⁻², joule J = N m, watt W = J s⁻¹.
- Near the Earth's surface, the acceleration due to gravity is g ≈ 9.8 m s⁻² (9.81 is also common; use whichever the question gives).
- Weight is a force, W = mg, measured in newtons. Mass is measured in kilograms. Do not confuse them.
- Check every answer for consistent units. For example, √(l/g) has units of time, and √(k/m) for a spring has units s⁻¹.

Scalars and vectors
- A scalar has size only (mass, time, speed, distance, energy). A vector has size and direction (displacement, velocity, acceleration, force, momentum).
- Speed is the magnitude of velocity; distance travelled is not the same as the magnitude of displacement (a lap of a track has zero displacement).
- In two dimensions write vectors as ai + bj or as column vectors. The magnitude of ai + bj is √(a² + b²) and its direction makes angle arctan(b/a) with i (taking care with the quadrant).
- Resolving: a force F at angle θ to the x-axis has components F cos θ and F sin θ.

Newton's laws (previewed)
- First: a particle remains at rest or moves with constant velocity unless a resultant force acts.
- Second: resultant force = mass × acceleration, F = ma (a vector equation).
- Third: if A exerts a force on B, then B exerts an equal and opposite force on A.

Method for any problem
- Draw a large, clear diagram showing every force on each body.
- Choose directions and axes, and state your modelling assumptions.
- Resolve and write equations, then solve and check units and limiting cases.

Exam tips: Dynamics and Relativity questions assume these basics without comment, so practise drawing force diagrams quickly and accurately.

Kinematics describes motion without asking what causes it. The key quantities are displacement, velocity and acceleration.

Definitions (one dimension)
- Displacement x(t) from a fixed origin; velocity v = dx/dt; acceleration a = dv/dt = d²x/dt².
- When a is given as a function of x, use the chain rule: a = dv/dt = v dv/dx.
- Going the other way, integrate: v = ∫ a dt, x = ∫ v dt, with constants fixed by initial conditions.
- On a velocity–time graph, the gradient is the acceleration and the (signed) area under the graph is the displacement.

Constant acceleration (the suvat equations)
With initial velocity u, final velocity v, acceleration a, time t and displacement s:
- v = u + at
- s = ut + ½at²
- s = vt − ½at²
- s = ½(u + v)t
- v² = u² + 2as
These hold only if the acceleration is constant. Example: a car moving at 20 m/s brakes with deceleration 4 m/s². It stops after t = 20/4 = 5 s, having travelled s = 20²/(2 × 4) = 50 m.

Variable acceleration
- Example: a = 6t m/s² with the particle starting from rest at the origin. Then v = 3t² and x = t³.
- Example: a = −4x (a simple harmonic acceleration, see later). Using v dv/dx = −4x gives v² = u² − 4x², so a particle with speed u at the origin turns round at x = ±u/2.

Motion in two and three dimensions
- Position vector r(t), velocity v = dr/dt, acceleration a = dv/dt, each found component by component.
- Example: r = (t², 3t) gives v = (2t, 3), a = (2, 0).

Projectiles (no air resistance)
- Take axes horizontal x and vertical y, with gravity −g j. Launch speed u at angle α above the horizontal.
- Horizontal: constant velocity u cos α, so x = ut cos α.
- Vertical: constant acceleration −g, so y = ut sin α − ½gt².
- Time of flight (back to launch height): 2u sin α/g. Range: u² sin 2α/g, maximal at α = 45°. Greatest height: u² sin²α/(2g).
- Trajectory: eliminating t, y = x tan α − gx²/(2u² cos²α), a parabola.
- Example: u = 20 m/s, α = 30°, g = 9.8 m/s². Time of flight 2.04 s, range ≈ 35.3 m, greatest height ≈ 5.10 m.
- Complementary angles α and 90° − α give the same range (sin 2α is the same).

Relative motion
- The velocity of A relative to B is v_A − v_B. Problems about interception or closest approach are easiest in B's frame.

Exam tips: before using suvat, check that the acceleration really is constant; for variable acceleration, decide whether you need a(t) (integrate in t) or a(x) (use v dv/dx).

A particle is in equilibrium when the resultant force on it is zero. Then it stays at rest (or moves with constant velocity). This lecture is about finding unknown forces from that condition.

The condition
- Vector form: ΣF = 0.
- In practice, resolve in two perpendicular directions and set each sum to zero. Choose directions that make the algebra easy, for example along and perpendicular to a slope, or perpendicular to an unknown force so that it drops out.
- Three forces in equilibrium form a closed triangle when drawn head to tail (the triangle of forces).
- Lami's theorem (an A-level shortcut, not an item in the Part IA schedule): if three forces F₁, F₂, F₃ keep a particle in equilibrium and αᵢ is the angle between the other two, then F₁/sin α₁ = F₂/sin α₂ = F₃/sin α₃.

Common forces
- Weight mg, vertically down.
- Normal reaction R, perpendicular to the surface of contact.
- Tension in a string (pulling away from the particle along the string); thrust in a rod can push or pull.
- Friction, along the surface, opposing the motion or the tendency to move.

Friction
- Coulomb's model: friction F satisfies F ≤ μR, where μ is the coefficient of friction.
- If the particle is on the point of moving (limiting equilibrium) or actually sliding, F = μR.
- A particle on a rough slope of angle α with no other forces stays put if tan α ≤ μ and is on the point of slipping when tan α = μ.
- Friction is not always at its maximum. In equilibrium, find F from the equations, then check F ≤ μR.

Worked example 1: two strings
A 10 kg mass hangs from two light strings making angles 30° and 60° with the horizontal. Take g = 9.8.
- Horizontally: T₁ cos 30° = T₂ cos 60°, so T₂ = √3 T₁.
- Vertically: T₁ sin 30° + T₂ sin 60° = 98, so T₁/2 + 3T₁/2 = 98.
- Hence T₁ = 49 N and T₂ = 49√3 ≈ 84.9 N. The steeper string carries more of the load.

Worked example 2: rough slope
A 5 kg block rests on a slope of 30° with μ = 0.4. Normal reaction R = 5g cos 30° ≈ 42.4 N, so maximum friction ≈ 17.0 N. The weight component down the slope is 5g sin 30° = 24.5 N.
- Since 24.5 > 17.0, the block will slip unless helped. The least force up the slope that holds it is 24.5 − 17.0 ≈ 7.5 N (friction acting up the slope).
- The greatest force up the slope before it slides upwards is 24.5 + 17.0 ≈ 41.5 N (friction now acting down the slope).

Strings and pulleys
- A light inextensible string over a smooth pulley has the same tension on both sides.
- A string can only pull; if your answer gives negative tension, the string is slack and the model has changed.

Exam tips: draw the diagram large, mark every force with an arrow, and say which way friction acts; in limiting equilibrium state "F = μR" explicitly.

A rigid body can rotate, so for equilibrium the forces must balance and must have no net turning effect.

Moments
- The moment of a force F about a point O is the force times the perpendicular distance from O to its line of action. Anticlockwise and clockwise moments have opposite signs.
- In vector form, the moment about O of F acting at r is r × F.
- A couple is a pair of equal and opposite forces with different lines of action. It has zero resultant force but a non-zero moment, the same about every point.

Conditions for equilibrium
- The resultant force is zero (resolve in two directions), and
- the total moment about any one point is zero.
- Taking moments about a point through which unknown forces act eliminates them, which is usually the quickest route.
- If three non-parallel forces keep a body in equilibrium, their lines of action meet at a point.

Centre of mass
- The weight of a body acts at its centre of mass. For a uniform rod it is the midpoint; for a uniform rectangular lamina the centre; for a uniform triangular lamina the centroid, two-thirds of the way from each vertex to the midpoint of the opposite side.
- For a composite body: x̄ = Σmᵢxᵢ/Σmᵢ (and similarly ȳ).
- A body suspended freely from a point hangs with its centre of mass vertically below that point.

Worked example 1: beam on supports
A uniform beam of length 4 m and mass 20 kg rests on supports at its ends. A person of mass 60 kg stands 1 m from the left end. Take g = 9.8.
- Moments about the left support: 4R_right = 20g × 2 + 60g × 1 = 100g, so R_right = 25g = 245 N.
- Vertically: R_left + R_right = 80g, so R_left = 55g = 539 N.
- Check by moments about the right end: 4R_left = 20g × 2 + 60g × 3 = 220g, so R_left = 55g.

Worked example 2: the ladder
A uniform ladder of length L and weight W rests against a smooth vertical wall, with its foot on rough horizontal ground (coefficient μ), at angle θ to the horizontal.
- Forces: W at the midpoint, normal reaction S from the wall (horizontal), normal reaction R and friction F at the ground.
- Vertically R = W; horizontally F = S.
- Moments about the foot: W(L/2) cos θ = S L sin θ, so S = (W/2) cot θ.
- The ladder does not slip if F ≤ μR, i.e. (W/2) cot θ ≤ μW, i.e. tan θ ≥ 1/(2μ). Steeper ladders are safer.

Toppling and sliding
- A block on a slope or pushed on the ground can either slide or topple. On the point of toppling, the normal reaction acts at the edge about which it would tip.
- Compare the force needed to make it slide (from friction) with the force needed to make it topple (from moments); the smaller one happens first.

Exam tips: always state the point you take moments about, and use one moments equation plus resolving rather than several moments equations, so that your equations are independent.

notes.h: Dynamics of particles, including projectiles with air resistance
notes.body:
Two lectures apply Newton's second law to moving particles. The second includes air resistance, which leads to differential equations rather than suvat.

Newton's second law
- Resultant force = mass × acceleration, F = ma, a vector equation. Resolve along and perpendicular to the motion.
- If the acceleration is constant, use the suvat equations; otherwise write a = dv/dt (or v dv/dx) and solve.

Connected particles
- Particles joined by a light inextensible string have equal speeds and accelerations along the string.
- Write F = ma separately for each particle, then solve simultaneously.
- Example (Atwood machine): masses 3 kg and 2 kg hang over a smooth pulley. For the 3 kg mass, 3g − T = 3a; for the 2 kg mass, T − 2g = 2a. Adding: a = g/5 ≈ 1.96 m/s², and T = 12g/5 ≈ 23.5 N (g = 9.8).
- In general a = (m₁ − m₂)g/(m₁ + m₂) and T = 2m₁m₂g/(m₁ + m₂).
- Lifts: a person of mass m in a lift accelerating upwards at a feels a reaction R = m(g + a).

Linear air resistance
- Model the resistance as −mkv (proportional to velocity, k a constant with units s⁻¹).
- Falling from rest: dv/dt = g − kv, so v = (g/k)(1 − e^(−kt)). The speed tends to the terminal speed g/k.
- Quadratic resistance (−cv² opposing motion) is a better model at higher speeds. Falling: m dv/dt = mg − cv², terminal speed √(mg/c), and v = V tanh(gt/V) with V the terminal speed.

Projectiles with linear air resistance
- Vector equation: dv/dt = −g j − kv. The horizontal and vertical motions separate.
- Horizontal (initial velocity u cos α): dẋ/dt = −kẋ, so ẋ = u cos α e^(−kt) and x = (u cos α/k)(1 − e^(−kt)). The horizontal distance can never exceed u cos α/k.
- Vertical (initial velocity w = u sin α): dẏ/dt = −g − kẏ, so ẏ = (w + g/k)e^(−kt) − g/k, which tends to −g/k (terminal velocity).
- The time to reach greatest height is (1/k) ln(1 + kw/g), which is less than the drag-free value w/g. For small k it is about w/g − kw²/(2g²).
- The path is no longer a parabola: the descent is steeper than the ascent.

Method
- Write the vector equation of motion first, then split into components.
- Solve each first-order equation by separating variables or with an integrating factor.
- Check the limit k → 0 recovers the drag-free result.

Exam tips: state the direction of resistance (always opposite to velocity); in connected-particle problems write a separate equation for each body and check that tensions are positive.

Energy methods often give speeds without solving for the motion in detail.

Work
- The work done by a constant force F when its point of application moves through displacement s is F·s = Fs cos θ, θ being the angle between them.
- For a variable force in one dimension, W = ∫ F dx.
- Work done by friction on a sliding body is negative: it removes energy, and the energy lost is μR × distance for constant friction.
- Forces perpendicular to the motion (such as a normal reaction on a fixed surface) do no work.

Kinetic and potential energy
- Kinetic energy: ½mv².
- Gravitational potential energy near the Earth: mgh, measured from a chosen level.
- Elastic potential energy of a spring of stiffness k stretched by x: ½kx² (see the springs lecture).

The work–energy principle
- Work done by the resultant force = change in kinetic energy.
- If only conservative forces (gravity, springs) do work, total mechanical energy KE + PE is conserved.
- With non-conservative forces (friction, resistance, an engine): initial energy + work done by those forces = final energy.

Worked example 1: rough slope
A 2 kg block slides from rest 5 m down a slope of 30° with μ = 0.2 (g = 9.8).
- Loss of PE: mg × 5 sin 30° = 49 J.
- Friction μmg cos 30° ≈ 3.39 N acts over 5 m, doing about 17.0 J of work against the motion.
- ½ × 2 × v² ≈ 49 − 17.0 = 32.0, so v ≈ 5.66 m/s.

Power
- Power is the rate of doing work: P = dW/dt. For a force F acting on a body moving at speed v in its direction, P = Fv. Units: watts.
- A vehicle's engine working at power P produces a driving force P/v.
- At maximum (steady) speed on the level the driving force equals the resistance R, so v_max = P/R. Example: P = 30 kW, R = 750 N gives 40 m/s.
- Up a slope of angle α, v_max = P/(R + mg sin α). Example: m = 1000 kg, sin α = 1/20, so 30000/(750 + 490) ≈ 24.2 m/s.

Worked example 2: a stone thrown upwards
A stone is thrown at 14 m/s from a cliff 20 m high. By energy, its speed on hitting the sea is √(14² + 2 × 9.8 × 20) = √588 ≈ 24.2 m/s, whatever the direction of throw (ignoring air resistance).

Why energy methods help
- They give speeds directly from positions without needing time.
- They do not give directions or times, so you may still need Newton's second law.

Exam tips: list every form of energy at the start and the end, and every force that does work in between; be careful with signs when a body moves against friction or resistance.

Momentum methods are ideal for collisions, explosions and short sharp forces, where the forces are large and hard to describe but act briefly.

Momentum and impulse
- Momentum is p = mv, a vector, with units kg m s⁻¹ (equivalently N s).
- Impulse of a force is I = ∫ F dt; for a constant force I = FΔt.
- Impulse–momentum principle: impulse = change in momentum, I = mv − mu.
- Example: a 0.15 kg ball hits a wall at 20 m/s and rebounds at 15 m/s. Impulse from the wall has magnitude 0.15 × (15 + 20) = 5.25 N s (directions matter).

Conservation of momentum
- If no external impulse acts on a system, its total momentum is conserved. In a collision between two bodies, the internal forces are equal and opposite (Newton's third law), so their impulses cancel.
- Holds in collisions (whether or not kinetic energy is conserved) and in explosions (two bodies moving apart from rest have equal and opposite momenta).

Newton's experimental law (restitution)
- For a direct collision: speed of separation = e × speed of approach, where 0 ≤ e ≤ 1 is the coefficient of restitution.
- e = 1: perfectly elastic, kinetic energy conserved. e = 0: the bodies coalesce (move together).
- For a ball hitting a fixed wall at speed u perpendicular to it, it rebounds at eu. A ball dropped from height h onto a floor rebounds to height e²h.
- For an oblique impact with a smooth wall, the component of velocity parallel to the wall is unchanged and the perpendicular component is multiplied by e and reversed.

Worked example
A 2 kg ball moving at 6 m/s hits a 1 kg ball at rest; e = 0.5. Let the final velocities be v₁ and v₂ (same direction as the original motion).
- Momentum: 2 × 6 = 2v₁ + v₂, so 2v₁ + v₂ = 12.
- Restitution: v₂ − v₁ = 0.5 × 6 = 3.
- Subtracting: 3v₁ = 9, so v₁ = 3 m/s and v₂ = 6 m/s.
- Kinetic energy before: ½ × 2 × 36 = 36 J. After: ½ × 2 × 9 + ½ × 1 × 36 = 27 J. So 9 J is lost (to heat, sound and deformation).

Common slips
- Momentum is a vector: choose a positive direction and give velocities signs.
- Kinetic energy is not conserved unless e = 1.
- In restitution, use relative velocities with consistent signs: v₂ − v₁ = −e(u₂ − u₁).

Connection with energy
- Momentum conservation and energy considerations answer different questions: momentum gives velocities after impact (with e), energy gives the losses.

Exam tips: draw before-and-after diagrams with all velocities in the same assumed direction, then let the algebra decide the actual directions.

notes.h: Springs, strings and simple harmonic motion
notes.body:
This lecture introduces elastic strings and springs, and the simple harmonic motion they produce, which reappears throughout the Tripos.

Hooke's law
- The tension in a stretched spring or elastic string is proportional to its extension x: T = kx, where k is the stiffness.
- A-level texts often write T = λx/l, where l is the natural length and λ the modulus of elasticity (a force). Then k = λ/l. This modulus form is not an item in the Part IA schedule, which just names Hooke's law.
- A spring can also be compressed and push (thrust). An elastic string can only pull: when it is shorter than its natural length it is slack, with zero tension.
- Elastic potential energy stored: ½kx² = λx²/(2l). This is the work done in stretching it from natural length.

Simple harmonic motion (SHM)
- Definition: acceleration proportional to displacement from a fixed point and directed towards it: ẍ = −ω²x.
- General solution: x = a cos(ωt + φ) (or A cos ωt + B sin ωt), with amplitude a and period 2π/ω, independent of amplitude.
- Speed: v² = ω²(a² − x²). The maximum speed is aω, at the centre; the maximum acceleration is aω², at the extremes.

Mass on a spring
- Horizontal smooth surface: mẍ = −kx, so ω = √(k/m).
- Vertical: at equilibrium the extension is e = mg/k. Measuring x from the equilibrium position, mẍ = mg − k(e + x) = −kx, so the motion is again SHM with ω = √(k/m) about the equilibrium point.
- Example: m = 0.5 kg, k = 50 N/m, amplitude 0.1 m. Then ω = 10 rad/s, period 2π/10 ≈ 0.63 s, maximum speed 1 m/s, maximum acceleration 10 m/s².

Elastic strings and incomplete SHM
- With an elastic string, the motion is SHM only while the string is taut. Once it goes slack, the particle moves freely under gravity. Many problems combine the two stages, using energy to link them.

Simple pendulum
- A particle on a light string of length l: lθ̈ = −g sin θ. For small θ, sin θ ≈ θ, giving SHM with ω = √(g/l) and period 2π√(l/g). A 1 m pendulum has period about 2.0 s.
- For large amplitudes the period is longer, and the motion is not exactly simple harmonic.

Energy in SHM
- For a spring, ½mv² + ½kx² is constant, equal to ½ka². Differentiating gives back mẍ = −kx.

Exam tips: always find the equilibrium position first and measure displacement from it; check whether an elastic string is taut throughout the motion.

The last lecture covers circular motion, which is the starting point for orbits and rotating frames in Dynamics and Relativity.

Angular speed and acceleration
- For motion on a circle of radius r, angular speed ω = dθ/dt and speed v = rω.
- Even at constant speed the velocity changes direction, so there is an acceleration towards the centre of magnitude v²/r = rω².
- If the speed changes, there is also a tangential acceleration r dω/dt = dv/dt.
- Newton's second law: the resultant force towards the centre must equal mv²/r. This is not a separate "centripetal force"; it is supplied by real forces such as tension, friction, a normal reaction or gravity.

Horizontal circles
- Car on a flat bend: friction provides mv²/r, so the car does not skid if v²/(rg) ≤ μ.
- Banked track at angle θ with no friction: N cos θ = mg and N sin θ = mv²/r, so tan θ = v²/(rg). At this speed no friction is needed.
- Conical pendulum: a particle on a string of length l moves in a horizontal circle with the string at angle α to the vertical. T cos α = mg and T sin α = mω²(l sin α), so T = mω²l and cos α = g/(ω²l). This needs ω² > g/l.

Vertical circles
- Use energy for the speed and the radial equation for the tension or reaction.
- Particle on a string of length l, speed u at the bottom. At angle θ from the downward vertical: v² = u² − 2gl(1 − cos θ) and T − mg cos θ = mv²/l, so T = mu²/l − 2mg + 3mg cos θ.
- The tension is least at the top (θ = π), where T = mu²/l − 5mg. The particle completes the circle only if u² ≥ 5gl.
- If 2gl < u² < 5gl, the string goes slack above the horizontal and the particle then moves as a projectile. If u² ≤ 2gl, it simply swings back and forth below the horizontal.
- A particle on a light rigid rod (which can push) completes the circle if u² > 4gl, since it only needs positive speed at the top.

Leaving a surface
- A particle slides from rest at the top of a smooth sphere of radius a. At angle θ from the vertical, v² = 2ga(1 − cos θ) and mg cos θ − R = mv²/a.
- It leaves the surface when R = 0, i.e. g cos θ = 2g(1 − cos θ), so cos θ = 2/3.

Exam tips: in vertical circle questions, write the energy equation and the radial equation separately, then set T = 0 or R = 0 to find where contact is lost.

cards.b: Of negligible mass. A light string has the same tension throughout (if nothing acts along it).
Does not stretch, so particles joined by the string share the same speed and acceleration.
Frictionless. A smooth pulley leaves the tension equal on both sides.
A particle has negligible size and cannot rotate; a rigid body has size and fixed shape, so moments matter.
1 N = 1 kg m s⁻²: the force that gives 1 kg an acceleration of 1 m s⁻².
Mass (kg) measures amount of matter; weight is the gravitational force mg on it, in newtons.

cards.f: Who should attend the Part IA Mechanics course?
cards.b: Students with limited A-level (or equivalent) mechanics; it is non-examinable but is assumed by Dynamics and Relativity.

cards.f: Acceleration as a function of position
cards.b: a = v dv/dx (chain rule), useful when a is given in terms of x.
v² = u² + 2as (constant acceleration only).
The displacement (signed area); the gradient is the acceleration.

cards.f: Range of a projectile on level ground
cards.b: u² sin 2α/g, greatest at α = 45°; angles α and 90° − α give the same range.
u² sin²α/(2g), reached at time u sin α/g.
y = x tan α − gx²/(2u² cos²α).

cards.f: Stopping distance from 20 m/s at 4 m/s² deceleration
cards.b: 50 m (v² = u² + 2as), taking 5 s.

cards.f: Condition for equilibrium of a particle
cards.b: Resultant force zero: resolve in two perpendicular directions and set each sum to zero.
F ≤ μR; F = μR when sliding or on the point of sliding (limiting equilibrium).

cards.f: When does a block on a rough slope begin to slip (no other forces)?
cards.b: When tan α = μ, α being the slope angle.
For three forces in equilibrium, each force divided by the sine of the angle between the other two is the same. (A-level shortcut; not a Part IA schedule item.)
Three forces in equilibrium, drawn head to tail, form a closed triangle.

cards.f: Tension in a string over a smooth pulley
cards.b: The same on both sides (light string, smooth pulley).

cards.f: Negative tension in your answer means...
cards.b: The string is slack (strings cannot push), so the assumed configuration is wrong.

cards.f: Moment of a force about a point
cards.b: Force × perpendicular distance from the point to its line of action (r × F in vector form).

cards.f: Conditions for equilibrium of a rigid body
cards.b: Resultant force zero and total moment zero about any one point.
Two equal, opposite, parallel forces not in line: zero resultant force but a moment that is the same about every point.
Their lines of action must pass through a single point.

cards.f: Ladder (smooth wall, rough floor μ) does not slip if...
cards.b: tan θ ≥ 1/(2μ), θ the angle with the horizontal (uniform ladder).

cards.f: Centre of mass of a composite body
cards.b: x̄ = Σmᵢxᵢ/Σmᵢ, ȳ = Σmᵢyᵢ/Σmᵢ.

cards.f: Centre of mass of a uniform triangular lamina
cards.b: At the centroid: two-thirds of the way along each median from the vertex.
a = (m₁ − m₂)g/(m₁ + m₂), tension T = 2m₁m₂g/(m₁ + m₂).

cards.f: Reaction on a person in a lift accelerating upwards at a
cards.b: R = m(g + a).

cards.f: Fall from rest with linear resistance mkv
cards.b: v = (g/k)(1 − e^(−kt)), terminal speed g/k.

cards.f: Terminal speed with quadratic resistance cv²
Horizontal distance of a projectile with linear drag
cards.b: x = (u cos α/k)(1 − e^(−kt)), never exceeding u cos α/k.

cards.f: Time to greatest height with linear drag
cards.b: (1/k) ln(1 + kw/g), w the initial vertical speed; less than w/g.
Always opposite to the velocity (relative to the air).

cards.f: Work done by a constant force
cards.b: F·s = Fs cos θ, θ the angle between force and displacement.
Work done by the resultant force equals the change in kinetic energy.

cards.f: Power of a force on a moving body
cards.b: P = Fv (force in direction of motion times speed); units watts.

cards.f: Maximum speed on the level with engine power P and resistance R
cards.b: v_max = P/R (driving force P/v balances R).
When only conservative forces (gravity, elastic forces) do work.
Not on a body moving along a fixed surface, since they are perpendicular to the motion.

cards.f: Speed of a stone thrown at 14 m/s from a 20 m cliff, on hitting the sea
cards.b: √(14² + 2 × 9.8 × 20) ≈ 24.2 m/s, independent of direction (no air resistance).
Impulse ∫F dt equals the change in momentum mv − mu.
Speed of separation = e × speed of approach, 0 ≤ e ≤ 1.
e = 1: perfectly elastic (KE conserved). e = 0: bodies coalesce.

cards.f: Rebound height of a ball dropped from h
cards.b: e²h (rebound speed is e times impact speed).

cards.f: Oblique impact with a smooth wall
cards.b: Parallel component unchanged; perpendicular component reversed and multiplied by e.
When no external impulse acts on the system, e.g. in collisions and explosions.
kg m s⁻¹, equivalently N s.
T = kx, or (A-level form, not in the Part IA schedule) T = λx/l with λ the modulus of elasticity and l the natural length (k = λ/l).
½kx² = λx²/(2l).
ẍ = −ω²x: acceleration proportional to displacement, directed towards the centre.
v² = ω²(a² − x²); maximum aω at the centre.

cards.f: Period of a mass on a spring
cards.b: 2π√(m/k), the same whether horizontal or vertical (vertical oscillation is about the equilibrium point).

cards.f: Period of a simple pendulum (small swings)
cards.b: 2π√(l/g); about 2.0 s for l = 1 m.
A spring can push or pull; an elastic string goes slack (zero tension) when shorter than its natural length.
v²/r = rω², directed towards the centre.

cards.f: Banked track with no friction needed
cards.b: tan θ = v²/(rg).
T = mω²l and cos α = g/(ω²l), possible only if ω² > g/l.

cards.f: Condition to complete a vertical circle on a string
cards.b: Speed u at the bottom with u² ≥ 5gl.

cards.f: Condition to complete a vertical circle on a light rod
cards.b: u² > 4gl (only positive speed at the top is needed, since a rod can push).

cards.f: Where does a particle leave a smooth sphere starting from rest at the top?
cards.b: Where cos θ = 2/3, θ measured from the upward vertical.

cards.f: Car on a flat bend: no skidding condition
cards.b: v²/(rg) ≤ μ (friction supplies mv²/r).

questions.q: Which of these is a vector quantity?
questions.why: Momentum mv has a direction. Kinetic energy, speed and mass all have size only, so they are scalars; speed is the magnitude of the velocity vector.

questions.q: In a mechanics model, what does it mean to say a string is light and inextensible?
options: It has negligible mass and does not stretch
It has negligible mass and can stretch elastically
It can push as well as pull
It is frictionless where it touches a pulley
questions.why: Light means negligible mass and inextensible means no stretching, so connected particles move together. A string that stretches is elastic, not inextensible; no string can push (only rods can); and frictionless contact is described by calling the pulley smooth.

questions.q: Explain the difference between mass and weight, give the SI units of each, and state the weight of a 70 kg person on the Earth's surface (g = 9.8 m s⁻²).
markScheme: Mass is the amount of matter / inertia, a scalar, in kg
Weight is the gravitational force on the body, a vector acting downwards
Weight in newtons, W = mg
questions.modelAnswer: Mass measures the amount of matter in a body (its inertia, its resistance to acceleration). It is a scalar measured in kilograms and is the same everywhere. Weight is the gravitational force on the body, W = mg, a vector acting vertically downwards, measured in newtons; it depends on the local gravitational field. A 70 kg person on the Earth's surface has weight 70 × 9.8 = 686 N.

questions.q: A particle is projected at 20 m/s at 30° above the horizontal on level ground (g = 9.8 m/s², no air resistance). What is its range?
questions.why: Range = u² sin 2α/g = 400 × sin 60°/9.8 ≈ 35.3 m. 40.8 m is u²/g, the maximum range (at 45°); 20.4 m is u² sin 30°/g, using sin α instead of sin 2α; and 5.1 m is the greatest height, not the range.

questions.q: A particle starts from rest at the origin with acceleration a = 6t m/s². Where is it at t = 2 s?
questions.why: Integrating, v = 3t² and x = t³, so x(2) = 8 m. 12 m is the velocity at t = 2 (3 × 4 m/s), not the position; 24 m wrongly uses suvat with a = 12 as if constant (½ × 12 × 4); and 16 m comes from forgetting to halve when integrating 6t (v = 6t², so x = 2t³).

questions.q: A ball is thrown at speed u at angle α above the horizontal from level ground. Ignoring air resistance, derive expressions for the time of flight, the range and the greatest height.
markScheme: Horizontal: x = ut cos α; vertical: y = ut sin α − ½gt²
Time of flight from y = 0: t = 2u sin α/g
Range = u cos α × 2u sin α/g = u² sin 2α/g
Greatest height when vertical velocity u sin α − gt = 0, t = u sin α/g
H = u² sin²α/(2g)
questions.modelAnswer: Horizontally the velocity is constant, u cos α, so x = ut cos α. Vertically the acceleration is −g, so y = ut sin α − ½gt². The ball lands when y = 0 with t > 0: t = 2u sin α/g (time of flight). The range is x at that time: u cos α × 2u sin α/g = 2u² sin α cos α/g = u² sin 2α/g. The greatest height occurs when the vertical velocity u sin α − gt is zero, i.e. t = u sin α/g, giving H = u sin α × u sin α/g − ½g(u sin α/g)² = u² sin²α/(2g).

questions.q: A 5 kg block rests on a rough slope inclined at 30°, with μ = 0.4 (g = 9.8 m/s²). What is the least force parallel to the slope, acting up the slope, that prevents it slipping down?
questions.why: The weight component down the slope is 24.5 N and maximum friction is 0.4 × 5 × 9.8 cos 30° ≈ 17.0 N, so a push of 24.5 − 17.0 ≈ 7.5 N is needed. 24.5 N ignores friction altogether; 41.5 N is the force at which the block would start moving up the slope; and friction alone is not enough because tan 30° ≈ 0.577 exceeds μ = 0.4.

questions.q: A particle of weight W hangs in equilibrium from two light strings, each making 45° with the horizontal. What is the tension in each string?
questions.why: By symmetry the tensions are equal, and vertically 2T sin 45° = W, so T = W/(2 × 1/√2) = W/√2. W/2 would be right only if both strings were vertical; W comes from treating sin 45° as 1/2; and √2 W comes from T sin 45° = W, which forgets that the two strings share the load.

questions.q: A 10 kg mass hangs from two light strings making angles of 30° and 60° with the horizontal. Find the tension in each string (g = 9.8 m/s²).
markScheme: Diagram with tensions T₁ (30° string) and T₂ (60° string) and weight 98 N
Horizontal: T₁ cos 30° = T₂ cos 60°, so T₂ = √3 T₁
Vertical: T₁ sin 30° + T₂ sin 60° = 98
Solves: 2T₁ = 98, T₁ = 49 N
questions.modelAnswer: Let T₁ be the tension in the string at 30° and T₂ in the string at 60°. Resolving horizontally: T₁ cos 30° = T₂ cos 60°, so (√3/2)T₁ = T₂/2 and T₂ = √3 T₁. Resolving vertically: T₁ sin 30° + T₂ sin 60° = 10 × 9.8 = 98, i.e. T₁/2 + √3 T₁ × √3/2 = T₁/2 + 3T₁/2 = 2T₁ = 98. So T₁ = 49 N and T₂ = 49√3 ≈ 84.9 N. (Lami's theorem, an A-level shortcut rather than a schedule item, gives the same: the angle opposite T₁ is 150°, opposite T₂ is 120°, opposite the weight is 90°.)

questions.q: A uniform beam 4 m long and of mass 20 kg rests on supports at its ends. A 60 kg person stands 1 m from the left end. What is the reaction at the right-hand support (g = 9.8 m/s²)?
questions.why: Moments about the left support: 4R = 20g × 2 + 60g × 1 = 100g, so R = 25g = 245 N. 539 N is the left-hand reaction; 392 N (40g) is half the total weight, which ignores where the person stands; and 784 N is the total weight.

questions.q: A uniform ladder rests against a smooth vertical wall with its foot on rough ground, coefficient of friction μ = 0.5. What is the smallest angle with the horizontal at which it can rest without slipping?
questions.why: The condition is tan θ ≥ 1/(2μ) = 1, so θ ≥ 45°. 30° gives tan θ ≈ 0.58 < 1, so the ladder would slip; 60° is safe but is not the smallest angle; and 26.6° (tan θ = 0.5 = μ) comes from forgetting the factor 2 that arises because the weight acts at the midpoint.

questions.q: A uniform ladder of length L and weight W rests against a smooth vertical wall, with its foot on rough horizontal ground (coefficient μ), making angle θ with the horizontal. Show that it is in equilibrium only if tan θ ≥ 1/(2μ).
markScheme: Diagram: W at midpoint, S horizontal at wall, R and F at the foot
Resolving: R = W and F = S
Moments about the foot: W(L/2) cos θ = S L sin θ
S = (W/2) cot θ, so F = (W/2) cot θ
F ≤ μR gives cot θ ≤ 2μ, i.e. tan θ ≥ 1/(2μ)
questions.modelAnswer: Forces: the weight W at the midpoint; the normal reaction S from the smooth wall, horizontal; the normal reaction R and friction F (towards the wall) at the foot. Resolving vertically, R = W; horizontally, F = S. Taking moments about the foot: the weight has moment W × (L/2) cos θ and S has moment S × L sin θ in the opposite sense, so S = (W/2) cot θ. Hence F = (W/2) cot θ. For equilibrium friction must satisfy F ≤ μR = μW, so (W/2) cot θ ≤ μW, i.e. cot θ ≤ 2μ, i.e. tan θ ≥ 1/(2μ).

questions.q: Masses of 3 kg and 2 kg hang on either side of a smooth pulley, connected by a light inextensible string (g = 9.8 m/s²). What is the tension in the string?
questions.why: Solving 3g − T = 3a and T − 2g = 2a gives a = g/5 and T = 12g/5 = 23.52 N. 19.6 N and 29.4 N are the weights of the masses (the tension must lie strictly between them); 24.5 N is the plain average of the two weights, which the equations of motion do not give.

questions.q: A particle falls from rest with air resistance mkv. What happens to its speed?
options: It increases towards g/k but never exceeds it
It reaches g/k after time 1/k and then stays constant
It increases to a maximum and then decreases
questions.why: Solving dv/dt = g − kv gives v = (g/k)(1 − e^(−kt)), which approaches the terminal speed g/k from below. Without limit would mean no resistance; the exponential never actually reaches g/k in finite time (after time 1/k it is only about 63% of it); and the speed is always increasing since g − kv > 0 while v < g/k.

questions.q: A particle of mass m falls from rest under gravity with air resistance of magnitude mkv. Find v(t) and the distance fallen in time t, and state the terminal speed.
markScheme: Equation of motion dv/dt = g − kv
Separates or uses integrating factor: v = (g/k)(1 − e^(−kt))
Terminal speed g/k
Integrates: distance = (g/k)t − (g/k²)(1 − e^(−kt))
Checks small k or small t limit gives ½gt²
questions.modelAnswer: Taking downwards as positive, m dv/dt = mg − mkv, so dv/dt = g − kv. Multiplying by e^(kt): d(ve^(kt))/dt = ge^(kt), so ve^(kt) = (g/k)e^(kt) + C; with v(0) = 0, C = −g/k and v = (g/k)(1 − e^(−kt)). As t → ∞, v → g/k, the terminal speed. Integrating again with x(0) = 0: x = (g/k)t − (g/k²)(1 − e^(−kt)). Check: for small kt, 1 − e^(−kt) ≈ kt − k²t²/2, so x ≈ (g/k)t − (g/k)t + ½gt² = ½gt², the drag-free result.

questions.q: A car's engine works at a constant 30 kW and the total resistance is 750 N. What is the car's maximum speed on level ground?
questions.why: At maximum speed the driving force P/v equals the resistance, so v = P/R = 30000/750 = 40 m/s. 25 m/s inverts the ratio, R/P with P in kilowatts (750/30); 4 m/s takes 30 kW as 3000 W (3000/750); and 22,500 m/s multiplies P (in kilowatts) by R instead of dividing.

questions.q: A block slides down a rough slope. Which statement about energy is correct?
options: The loss of potential energy equals the gain in kinetic energy plus the work done against friction
Mechanical energy is conserved because the slope is fixed
The normal reaction does work equal to the friction work
Kinetic energy gained equals potential energy lost, whatever the friction
questions.why: Friction does negative work, so PE lost = KE gained + work against friction. Mechanical energy is not conserved when friction acts, even on a fixed slope; the normal reaction is perpendicular to the motion and does no work; and equating KE gained to PE lost ignores the energy dissipated by friction.

questions.q: A 2 kg block is released from rest and slides 5 m down a rough slope inclined at 30°, with μ = 0.2 (g = 9.8 m/s²). Use an energy method to find its speed after 5 m.
markScheme: PE lost: 2 × 9.8 × 5 sin 30° = 49 J
Normal reaction 2 × 9.8 cos 30° ≈ 16.97 N; friction ≈ 3.39 N
Work against friction ≈ 3.39 × 5 ≈ 17.0 J
questions.modelAnswer: The block descends 5 sin 30° = 2.5 m vertically, so it loses potential energy 2 × 9.8 × 2.5 = 49 J. The normal reaction is R = 2 × 9.8 cos 30° ≈ 16.97 N, so friction is μR ≈ 3.39 N, and the work done against it over 5 m is about 16.97 J. By the work–energy principle, ½ × 2 × v² = 49 − 16.97 ≈ 32.03, so v² ≈ 32.0 and v ≈ 5.66 m/s.

questions.q: A 2 kg ball moving at 6 m/s collides directly with a stationary 1 kg ball; the coefficient of restitution is 0.5. What is the velocity of the 1 kg ball afterwards?
questions.why: Momentum gives 2v₁ + v₂ = 12 and restitution gives v₂ − v₁ = 3, so v₁ = 3 m/s and v₂ = 6 m/s. 3 m/s is the 2 kg ball's velocity; 4 m/s is the common velocity if they coalesced (e = 0); and 8 m/s is the result for a perfectly elastic collision (e = 1).

questions.q: A ball is dropped from a height of 2 m onto a floor with coefficient of restitution 0.5. To what height does it rebound?
questions.why: The rebound speed is e times the impact speed, so the height is e² × 2 = 0.25 × 2 = 0.5 m. 1 m multiplies the height by e instead of e²; 0.25 m is e² itself, not e²h; and 2 m would need e = 1.

questions.q: A 2 kg ball moving at 6 m/s collides directly with a stationary 1 kg ball, with coefficient of restitution 0.5. Find both velocities after impact and the loss of kinetic energy.
markScheme: Momentum: 2 × 6 = 2v₁ + v₂
Restitution: v₂ − v₁ = 0.5 × 6 = 3
Solves v₁ = 3 m/s, v₂ = 6 m/s (both in original direction)
KE before 36 J, after 9 + 18 = 27 J
Loss 9 J
questions.modelAnswer: Let v₁ and v₂ be the velocities of the 2 kg and 1 kg balls after impact, in the original direction of motion. Conservation of momentum: 2 × 6 + 1 × 0 = 2v₁ + v₂, so 2v₁ + v₂ = 12. Newton's experimental law: v₂ − v₁ = 0.5 × (6 − 0) = 3. Subtracting gives 3v₁ = 9, so v₁ = 3 m/s and v₂ = 6 m/s; both move in the original direction. Kinetic energy before: ½ × 2 × 6² = 36 J. After: ½ × 2 × 3² + ½ × 1 × 6² = 9 + 18 = 27 J. So 9 J of kinetic energy is lost.

questions.q: A 0.5 kg mass on a spring of stiffness 50 N/m oscillates with amplitude 0.1 m. What is its maximum speed?
questions.why: ω = √(k/m) = √100 = 10 rad/s, and the maximum speed is aω = 0.1 × 10 = 1 m/s. 10 is the value of ω in rad/s (and of the maximum acceleration aω² in m/s²), not a speed; 0.1 m/s is the amplitude; and 5 is ka = 50 × 0.1, the maximum spring force in newtons, not a speed.

questions.q: A particle hangs in equilibrium on a vertical spring of stiffness k, with static extension e. It is pulled down and released. About which point does it perform SHM, and with what angular frequency?
options: About the equilibrium position, with ω = √(k/m)
About the natural-length position, with ω = √(k/m)
About the equilibrium position, with ω = √(g/e) + √(k/m)
About the release point, with ω = √(mg/k)
questions.why: Measuring x from equilibrium, mẍ = mg − k(e + x) = −kx since ke = mg, so it is SHM about equilibrium with ω = √(k/m) (which also equals √(g/e)). The centre is not the natural-length position, because gravity shifts it; adding frequencies has no basis; and √(mg/k) has units of √length, so cannot be a frequency.

questions.q: A particle of mass m is attached to a vertical spring of stiffness k and hangs in equilibrium. Show that, measured from the equilibrium position, its vertical motion is simple harmonic, and find the period. If it is released from rest a distance d below equilibrium, find its maximum speed.
markScheme: Equilibrium extension e = mg/k
Equation with x below equilibrium: mẍ = mg − k(e + x)
Simplifies to ẍ = −(k/m)x: SHM with ω = √(k/m)
Period 2π√(m/k)
Amplitude d, maximum speed d√(k/m) at the equilibrium position
questions.modelAnswer: At equilibrium the spring force balances the weight: ke = mg, so the extension is e = mg/k. Let x be the displacement below equilibrium, so the extension is e + x. Newton's second law (downwards positive): mẍ = mg − k(e + x) = −kx, using ke = mg. So ẍ = −(k/m)x: simple harmonic motion about the equilibrium position with ω = √(k/m) and period 2π√(m/k). Released from rest at x = d, the amplitude is d (assuming the spring stays within its elastic range), and the maximum speed, at the equilibrium position, is dω = d√(k/m).

questions.q: A car travels round a banked track of radius 50 m at the speed for which no friction is needed. The bank angle θ satisfies tan θ = 0.2 (g = 9.8 m/s²). What is that speed?
questions.why: With no friction tan θ = v²/(rg), so v² = 0.2 × 50 × 9.8 = 98 and v ≈ 9.9 m/s. 98 is v², not v; 3.1 m/s comes from omitting g (√(0.2 × 50)); and 22 m/s corresponds to v²/(rg) = 1, i.e. a 45° bank.

questions.q: A particle on a light inextensible string of length l is given speed u at the bottom of a vertical circle. Which condition ensures it completes the circle with the string taut?
questions.why: At the top T = mu²/l − 5mg, which is non-negative only if u² ≥ 5gl. u² ≥ 4gl is the condition for a rigid rod, which can push; u² = 2gl only takes it to the horizontal; and u² ≥ gl is the condition on the speed at the top, not at the bottom.

questions.q: A conical pendulum consists of a particle of mass m on a light string of length l, moving in a horizontal circle with angular speed ω, with the string at angle α to the vertical. Find the tension and cos α, and show that this motion is possible only if ω² > g/l.
markScheme: Radius of circle l sin α; acceleration ω²l sin α towards the centre
Vertically: T cos α = mg
Horizontally: T sin α = mω²l sin α, so T = mω²l
cos α = mg/T = g/(ω²l)
cos α < 1 (α > 0) requires ω² > g/l
questions.modelAnswer: The particle moves in a horizontal circle of radius l sin α, so its acceleration is ω²l sin α towards the centre. Vertically there is no acceleration: T cos α = mg. Horizontally: T sin α = m ω² l sin α, and since sin α ≠ 0, T = mω²l. Then cos α = mg/T = g/(ω²l). For the string to be inclined we need 0 < cos α < 1, so g/(ω²l) < 1, i.e. ω² > g/l. (If ω² ≤ g/l the only possibility is the string hanging vertically.)

questions.q:
A particle of mass m is projected from the origin with speed u at angle α above the horizontal. It moves under gravity −g j and air resistance −mkv, where v is its velocity and k > 0 is constant.
(a) Write down the vector equation of motion and solve for the horizontal velocity and displacement. Show that the particle never travels more than u cos α/k horizontally. [6]
(b) Writing w = u sin α, find the vertical velocity and height as functions of t, and state the terminal velocity. [6]
(c) Find the time T at which the particle reaches its greatest height, and show that for small k, T ≈ w/g − kw²/(2g²). Interpret this result. [8]
markScheme: (a) m dv/dt = −mg j − mkv, so dv/dt = −g j − kv
(a) ẋ = u cos α e^(−kt), x = (u cos α/k)(1 − e^(−kt)) < u cos α/k
(b) dẏ/dt = −g − kẏ, ẏ = (w + g/k)e^(−kt) − g/k
(b) y = ((w + g/k)/k)(1 − e^(−kt)) − gt/k; terminal velocity −(g/k) j
(c) ẏ = 0 gives e^(kT) = 1 + kw/g, T = (1/k) ln(1 + kw/g)
(c) Expands ln(1 + ε) ≈ ε − ε²/2 with ε = kw/g
(c) Interpretation: reaches top sooner than without drag (w/g), as resistance adds to gravity on the way up; k → 0 recovers w/g
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Newton's second law: m dv/dt = −mg j − mkv, so dv/dt = −g j − kv. Horizontally, dẋ/dt = −kẋ with ẋ(0) = u cos α, so ẋ = u cos α e^(−kt). Integrating with x(0) = 0: x = (u cos α/k)(1 − e^(−kt)). Since 1 − e^(−kt) < 1 for all t, x < u cos α/k: the horizontal distance is bounded.

(b) Vertically, dẏ/dt = −g − kẏ with ẏ(0) = w. Multiplying by e^(kt): d(ẏe^(kt))/dt = −ge^(kt), so ẏe^(kt) = −(g/k)e^(kt) + C, and ẏ(0) = w gives C = w + g/k. Hence ẏ = (w + g/k)e^(−kt) − g/k. Integrating with y(0) = 0: y = ((w + g/k)/k)(1 − e^(−kt)) − gt/k. As t → ∞, ẋ → 0 and ẏ → −g/k, so the terminal velocity is −(g/k) j (vertically downwards with speed g/k).

(c) At greatest height ẏ = 0: (w + g/k)e^(−kT) = g/k, so e^(kT) = (w + g/k)/(g/k) = 1 + kw/g and T = (1/k) ln(1 + kw/g). For small k, with ε = kw/g, ln(1 + ε) = ε − ε²/2 + O(ε³), so T = (1/k)(kw/g − k²w²/(2g²) + ...) = w/g − kw²/(2g²) + O(k²). Without resistance the time to the top is w/g; the correction is negative, so with air resistance the particle reaches its greatest height sooner. This is because on the way up resistance acts downwards, adding to gravity and slowing the upward motion faster. Setting k = 0 recovers the drag-free result, a useful check.

questions.q:
A particle P of mass m is attached to one end of a light inextensible string of length l, the other end of which is fixed at O. P hangs at rest and is then given a horizontal speed u.
(a) When OP makes angle θ with the downward vertical and the string is taut, find the speed v of P and the tension T in the string. [7]
(b) Show that P makes complete circles if and only if u² ≥ 5gl. [4]
(c) Now suppose u² = 3gl. Find the value of cos θ at which the string becomes slack, and the speed of P at that moment. Describe the subsequent motion. [6]
(d) How would the condition in (b) change if the string were replaced by a light rigid rod? Explain briefly. [3]
markScheme: (a) Energy: ½mv² = ½mu² − mgl(1 − cos θ), so v² = u² − 2gl(1 − cos θ)
(a) Radial equation: T − mg cos θ = mv²/l, giving T = mu²/l − 2mg + 3mg cos θ
(b) T decreases with θ, least at θ = π: T = mu²/l − 5mg; need T ≥ 0 so u² ≥ 5gl (conversely T > 0 everywhere ensures completion)
(c) T = mg(1 + 3 cos θ) = 0 gives cos θ = −1/3
(c) v² = gl/3 (equivalently −gl cos θ)
(c) Afterwards P moves as a projectile under gravity until the string becomes taut again
(d) A rod can push, so only v > 0 at top is needed: u² > 4gl
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) The tension is perpendicular to the motion, so does no work, and energy is conserved. P rises l(1 − cos θ), so ½mv² = ½mu² − mgl(1 − cos θ), giving v² = u² − 2gl(1 − cos θ). P moves on a circle of radius l, so the resultant force towards O is mv²/l: T − mg cos θ = mv²/l. Hence T = m(u² − 2gl + 2gl cos θ)/l + mg cos θ = mu²/l − 2mg + 3mg cos θ.

(b) T decreases as θ increases from 0 to π (cos θ decreases), so its least value is at the top, θ = π: T = mu²/l − 5mg. If u² ≥ 5gl then T ≥ 0 for all θ, the string stays taut (and v² = u² − 4gl > 0 at the top), so P completes the circle. If u² < 5gl then T would become negative before the top, which is impossible for a string: the string goes slack (or, if u² ≤ 2gl, P never rises above the level of O and swings back). So P makes complete circles if and only if u² ≥ 5gl.

(c) With u² = 3gl, T = 3mg − 2mg + 3mg cos θ = mg(1 + 3 cos θ), which is zero when cos θ = −1/3, i.e. θ ≈ 109.5°, above the level of O. There v² = 3gl − 2gl(1 + 1/3) = 3gl − 8gl/3 = gl/3, so v = √(gl/3). (Check: at T = 0 the radial equation gives v² = −gl cos θ = gl/3.) After this the string is slack, so P moves freely as a projectile under gravity alone, starting with speed √(gl/3) along the tangent to the circle (inclined upwards and back towards the vertical through O), following a parabola inside the circle until the string becomes taut again.

(d) A light rigid rod can push as well as pull, so the 'tension' is allowed to become negative (a thrust). The only requirement is that P still has positive speed at the top: v² = u² − 4gl > 0, i.e. u² > 4gl, a weaker condition than for a string.
